options.text: Ask the steering group to confirm whether the adopt-not-adapt principle should apply to reporting at all, given how strongly the HR business partners feel about the reports they rely on.
options.rationale: It reopens an approved decision before anyone has tested whether it causes a problem. The candidate choosing this mistakes the strength of a reaction for evidence that the principle is wrong.

options.text: Tell the HR business partners that the steering group's principle rules out custom reports, and that they should plan to work from the standard report set.
options.rationale: It applies the principle as a blanket refusal and ignores its legal and contractual exception. Some reports may meet that test, and refusing them unseen leaves the business partners convinced the principle is arbitrary.

questions.explanation: An approved design principle only aligns expectations when it is applied to real requests in front of the people making them. Each expectation should be tested against the principle's stated criteria, so stakeholders see why most requests fall away and which survive as genuine exceptions. Waving everything through, refusing everything or reopening the principle all avoid the one step that makes the principle credible to the people it constrains.
questions.mindset: A principle earns acceptance when people see it applied to their own requests.

questions.stem: Your hybrid project is replacing a brewing company's production-scheduling software. The equipment interfaces are baselined; scheduling features are released iteratively, and the first release is in a four-week pilot at one brewery, running alongside the old system. This morning you learn that the brewery's plant manager, pleased with the first week, plans to switch the old system off at the end of today's shift. What should you do?

options.text: Raise the switch-off plan at Thursday's weekly pilot review, where the plant manager and the product owner can agree measurable criteria for retiring the old system safely.
options.rationale: The review is the right forum for exit criteria, but it falls days after the switch-off. The candidate choosing this follows the project's normal rhythm when the stakeholder is about to act today on a mistaken view of what the pilot release is.

options.text: Email all pilot users today restating the pilot's terms, including the requirement to keep the old system running in parallel for the full four weeks.
options.rationale: It sends the right message through the wrong channel. A general email may not be read before the shift ends, and it does not engage the one person who has made the decision or find out why he thinks the release is ready.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to instruct the plant manager to keep the old system running, since the pilot terms were approved by the steering group at the outset.
options.rationale: It reaches for authority before explanation and adds a step when time is short. The plant manager's enthusiasm is a good sign; he needs to understand what a pilot release is, not to be overruled from above.

options.text: Call the plant manager now to explain that the pilot release is not yet cleared for sole use, and agree that the old system stays running until the pilot exit review.
options.rationale: He believes a pilot release is ready for production and is about to act on that belief within hours. Speaking to him directly, before the shift ends, corrects the expectation while the old system is still there to fall back on.

questions.explanation: When a stakeholder is about to take an irreversible step on a mistaken expectation, the response has to reach them, directly, before they act. Scheduled forums, broadcast messages and escalation all have their place, but each is slower or less personal than the moment allows. Correct the belief with the person making the decision, then use the normal routines to agree what happens next.
questions.mindset: When someone is about to act on a wrong belief, reach them before they act, not after.

questions.stem: Your hybrid project is introducing new warehouse workflows for a distribution company in the Netherlands. The handheld hardware rollout is planned and baselined, while workflow software is released every two weeks. The works council expects to be consulted on any change affecting employees' roles, and assumed this would happen once, on a final design. The team expected to release changes continuously. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Agree with the works council criteria that separate releases affecting roles, which need consultation, from those that do not, and plan releases around them.
options.rationale: Most fortnightly releases will not touch anyone's role. Agreeing where the line sits lets consultation happen for the changes that warrant it while everything else keeps moving, so both expectations survive.

options.text: Invite a works council representative to the fortnightly reviews, so that emerging role changes are seen well before they reach the consultation stage.
options.rationale: The council expected one look at a finished design; early sight of what is emerging replaces that with something more useful to them. Consultation then starts from changes they have already seen, not from surprises.

options.text: Hold all workflow releases until the full design is complete, then consult the works council once on the whole package, as it expected.
options.rationale: It meets the council's expectation by abandoning the iterative approach entirely. The candidate choosing this sees only one legitimate expectation in the room and gives up the feedback the project chose fortnightly releases to get.

options.text: Continue fortnightly releases and consult the works council afterwards on any change that turns out to have affected employees' roles.
options.rationale: Consultation after the change is not consultation. The candidate picking this protects the release cadence by overriding a formal right, which will damage trust and may breach the council's entitlement.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to seek a single advance consent from the works council covering all workflow changes the project might make over its lifetime.
options.rationale: Blanket consent for unknown changes asks the council to give up the right it is there to exercise. The candidate choosing this tries to make the expectation disappear rather than align it, and is likely to be refused.

questions.explanation: When a stakeholder's formal right is built around a single decision point and the delivery approach produces many small ones, neither expectation can simply win. The workable middle is to agree which changes trigger the right and to give the stakeholder early sight of what is emerging, so the right is exercised where it matters without stopping everything else. Abandoning the cadence, bypassing the right or asking for blanket consent each sacrifice one side's legitimate expectation to the other's.
questions.mindset: When two legitimate expectations collide, look for the line that lets both hold.

questions.stem: Midway through a terminal expansion at a regional airport, a new head of security joins the steering group. She tells you she expects to approve every design package before issue, as she did at her previous airport. The responsibility matrix, approved by the sponsor, shows security as consulted on design packages, with approval resting with the design authority. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Add her as an approver on all design packages, since a head of security's sign-off reduces the risk of security findings later in the project.
options.rationale: It changes decision rights the project manager does not own and adds a bottleneck to every package. The candidate choosing this mistakes reducing one risk for having the authority to redesign governance.

options.text: Meet her to understand which security risks are driving her expectation, and which of the design packages actually raise them.
options.rationale: A new stakeholder asking for a decision right is usually carrying a concern, and hers may be legitimate. Understanding it shows whether her need is approval of everything or meaningful influence over a few packages.

options.text: Explain that the approved responsibility matrix shows security as consulted, and send her the design review procedure for her reference.
options.rationale: It closes the conversation with a document and ignores the concern behind the request. The candidate picking this treats an approved matrix as the end of the matter when its owner may want to revisit it.

options.text: Take her request to the sponsor, as owner of the responsibility matrix, with your view of its likely impact on design review and the schedule.
options.rationale: Whether security gains approval rights is a governance decision, and the sponsor owns the matrix. Bringing the request with its consequences lets the person with authority decide rather than leaving the gap to fester.

options.text: Route design packages to her informally for comment before issue, without changing the responsibility matrix, to keep her on side.
options.rationale: It creates a shadow approval step with no accountability attached. She will reasonably come to expect a veto that the governance does not give her, which widens the gap it was meant to close.

questions.explanation: A stakeholder who arrives expecting a different decision right is usually carrying a concern, not just a habit, and the concern may be legitimate. Find out what is driving the expectation, then take any change to decision rights to whoever owns them, with the consequences laid out. Granting the right yourself, refusing by citing the matrix or creating an informal workaround all decide a governance question at the wrong level.
questions.mindset: Understand why someone wants a decision right, then let the owner of decision rights decide.

questions.stem: One agile team serves both the retail and commercial divisions of a bank, with a single product owner ordering the backlog by estimated customer value. For three months, retail items have mostly ranked higher. The commercial director, who expected roughly half of the team's capacity because both divisions fund it equally, has complained to the sponsor that his division is being ignored. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Show the commercial director how the product owner scores and orders items, using his division's recent items as worked examples.
options.rationale: The director cannot see the rule being applied, so the outcome looks like neglect. Walking through his own items shows whether the ordering is principled, and gives him a way to argue for his items on the same terms.

options.text: Agree with the product owner to split each sprint's capacity equally between retail and commercial items, so it matches the funding.
options.rationale: It imposes a funding-based split nobody with authority has chosen and abandons value ordering. The candidate choosing this resolves the complaint by making a governance decision at the wrong level.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to decide whether equal funding should mean a guaranteed share of capacity, and record the decision in the product's governance.
options.rationale: The director's expectation rests on an unstated rule that conflicts with the one in use. Only the sponsor can say which rule governs, and recording it stops the same disagreement returning each quarter.

options.text: Alternate sprints between the two divisions so each has a predictable turn, while keeping the product owner's ordering within each sprint.
options.rationale: It looks fair and keeps some ordering, but still substitutes a capacity rule nobody authorised. The candidate picking this answers the funding question without asking the person who owns it.

options.text: Ask the product owner to raise the ranking of the commercial division's top three items to restore the director's confidence in the process.
options.rationale: Adjusting rankings to appease one party undermines the ordering method and the product owner's credibility. It treats the symptom and confirms that complaining is how priority is won.

questions.explanation: Expectations about how shared capacity is divided often rest on an unstated rule — equal funding means an equal share — that conflicts with the rule actually being applied. Both rules need to be made explicit: the ordering method, so the disadvantaged party can see decisions are not arbitrary, and the funding question, so someone with authority decides whether a guaranteed share is wanted. Splitting or adjusting the backlog on the project's own initiative answers a governance question nobody has asked the right person.
questions.mindset: When people disagree about how something is shared, surface the rule each of them is using.

questions.stem: You are planning an office fit-out for an engineering consultancy. In interviews, partners described their expectations in general terms, and you want each turned into an acceptance criterion the handover can be tested against. Match each stated expectation to the criterion that makes it testable. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The head of the structures team says the open-plan floor must be quiet enough for people to concentrate.
The managing partner says there must be plenty of meeting space, without the constant hunt for a free room.
The office manager says a colleague who uses a wheelchair must be able to get everywhere the rest of the staff can.

options.text: Background noise in open-plan areas no higher than 45 dB(A) with the floor occupied
options.rationale: 'Quiet enough to concentrate' becomes a measured sound level under real conditions. It can be designed to, tested at handover and argued about with numbers rather than impressions.

options.text: At least one bookable meeting room for every 10 desks, with a booking system showing live availability
options.rationale: 'Plenty of space' and 'no hunting' are two separate complaints: too few rooms and no way to see which are free. A ratio plus visible availability turns both into checkable facts.

options.text: Step-free routes to every floor and room, with clear door openings of at least 850 mm
options.rationale: 'Get everywhere' becomes a route and a dimension that can be inspected. It tests the whole journey rather than individual rooms, which is what the office manager actually described.

options.text: Temperature held between 20 °C and 23 °C in all occupied zones during working hours
options.rationale: Not used. It is a perfectly testable comfort criterion, but nobody raised temperature. Adding criteria no stakeholder expressed inflates scope without aligning any expectation.

questions.explanation: A stated expectation such as 'quiet' or 'plenty of space' cannot be met or missed, so at handover it will be judged against whatever each person privately imagined. Converting each into a measurable criterion, agreed with the person who holds it, turns a feeling into something that can be designed to, tested and signed off. Every criterion should trace back to an expectation someone actually stated; a measurable criterion nobody asked for adds cost without aligning anything.
questions.mindset: If an expectation cannot be tested, it will be judged by memory at handover.

questions.stem: On an agile team building a parcel-tracking app, several stakeholders hold expectations that someone needs to reset. As the team's agile lead, you want each conversation held by the person accountable for the decision it depends on. Match each situation to the person who should hold the conversation. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A regional manager believes his delivery-slot filter will be added to the current sprint because he mentioned it to a developer.
A marketing director expects a firm points estimate today for a loyalty feature the developers have never discussed.
The sponsor's chief of staff expects the team to switch to one-week sprints next quarter so that it 'goes faster'.

options.text: The product owner
options.rationale: What enters the backlog, and whether anything displaces sprint work, is the product owner's call. A word with a developer is not a route into the sprint, and the product owner is the person who can say so with authority.

options.text: The developers who will build it
options.rationale: Estimates belong to the people doing the work. Only they can explain why an unrefined feature has no honest estimate yet and what refinement would be needed to produce one.

options.text: You, as the agile lead
options.rationale: Sprint length is a question about the team's process, which the agile lead coaches on. The expectation that shorter sprints mean faster delivery is a misunderstanding of what cadence is for, and correcting it is a coaching conversation.

options.text: The sponsor
options.rationale: Not used. None of these needs the sponsor's authority, and routing them upwards would take decisions away from the roles that own them and teach stakeholders to go over the team's head.

questions.explanation: An expectation is reset most effectively by the person accountable for the decision it depends on, because only they can explain it with authority and change it if it should change. In agile teams, backlog content belongs to the product owner, estimates to the people doing the work and process to the team supported by its agile lead. Routing every expectation gap through one person, or upwards to a sponsor, weakens the roles that are meant to own those decisions.
questions.mindset: Reset an expectation through the person who owns the decision it depends on.

questions.stem: You are managing a sewer replacement along a residential street. At a residents' meeting, three expectations were raised, each needing a different response. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Residents expect no work on Sundays, and the planning consent for the scheme already prohibits Sunday working. The project manager should
Residents expect the street to stay open throughout, but the main connection needs a three-week full closure next spring. The project manager should
Residents expect bin collections to continue as normal, which is possible only if the council's waste team agrees to a new collection time. The project manager should

options.text: confirm the commitment in writing in the next residents' bulletin, so that it is on record
options.rationale: The expectation already matches what the project must do. Putting it in writing turns a reassurance given in a meeting into a commitment residents can hold the project to, at no cost.

options.text: explain the closure now, with its dates, reason and diversion, well before it is booked
options.rationale: This expectation cannot be met. Explaining it months ahead, with the reason and the alternative, lets residents plan around it rather than discover it from a road sign.

options.text: agree the revised collection time with the council's waste team before telling residents what will happen
options.rationale: The expectation can be met, but only with a decision another party owns. Securing that decision first avoids promising residents something the waste team then declines.

options.text: record the expectation in the stakeholder register and review it if complaints are received
options.rationale: Not used. Each of these expectations calls for an active response now; waiting for complaints treats a known expectation as a risk that may never arise.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder expectations fall into different kinds, and each needs a different move: one that already matches the plan should be confirmed on record, one that cannot be met should be explained early with the reason and the alternative, and one that depends on a third party should be secured with that party before anything is promised. Sorting expectations by which kind they are, before responding, stops a project from over-promising, under-explaining or simply waiting.
questions.mindset: Before answering an expectation, work out whether it can be met, cannot be met or depends on someone else.

questions.stem: A supplier's contract for a new contact-centre telephony platform guarantees 99.5% availability, measured over each 30-day month with no exclusions. The contact-centre manager has told her team to expect 'no more than an hour of downtime a month'. Work out the figures below so that you can show her the gap.

blanks.label: Downtime the 99.5% guarantee permits in a 30-day month, in minutes
blanks.rationale: A 30-day month has 30 × 24 × 60 = 43,200 minutes. The guarantee allows 0.5% of that to be lost: 43,200 × 0.005 = 216 minutes, or 3.6 hours.

blanks.label: Availability the supplier would need to guarantee for no more than 60 minutes of downtime a month, as a percentage to two decimal places
blanks.rationale: Sixty minutes out of 43,200 is 0.139% downtime, so availability must be 100 − 0.139 = 99.861%, which rounds to 99.86%. A difference that looks tiny as a percentage is large in minutes.

blanks.label: How many times the manager's expected maximum the contract actually permits, to one decimal place
blanks.rationale: The contract permits 216 minutes against her expected 60: 216 ÷ 60 = 3.6. Her team is planning for under a third of the downtime the supplier is entitled to have.

questions.explanation: A service level stated as a percentage hides its meaning until it is converted into time over the measurement period, and stakeholders routinely read a high-sounding percentage as near-perfect. Translating it into minutes per period, and setting that beside what the stakeholder assumes, shows the gap before an outage does. The measurement period and any exclusions matter as much as the figure: the same percentage means different things measured monthly or annually.
questions.mindset: Translate a percentage into hours before anyone relies on it.

questions.stem: The roadmap for a ferry operator's booking app is shown with each item's current state. The commercial director wants to write one item into a partner agreement as a dated commitment for three weeks from today. The team releases at the end of every two-week sprint, and the current sprint ends in nine days. Select the item for which a dated commitment is defensible.

graphic.title: Now, Next and Later roadmap columns with four items and their current state
graphic.caption: Select an item. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Now — Multi-leg booking: in the current sprint, all stories built, final testing under way, due in the release in nine days
regions.rationale: The work is understood, almost finished and inside the team's own sprint, with a release before the date in question. It is the only item where the date rests on observed progress rather than on a forecast or on someone else's plan.

regions.label: Next — Partner fares API: estimated at 40–60 points; velocity has ranged from 25 to 30 points a sprint
regions.rationale: Even at the top of the velocity range, 40–60 points needs about two full sprints after the current one, which ends well beyond three weeks. The estimate itself is a range, so a single date would hide its uncertainty.

regions.label: Next — Group bookings: 20 points, fits in one sprint, but needs the payments team's API, which is not yet scheduled
regions.rationale: It is the tempting choice because it is small and well sized. But its date depends on another team's backlog that nobody has committed to, so promising it would commit the payments team without its agreement.

regions.label: Later — Loyalty points: idea stage, not yet refined or estimated
regions.rationale: An unrefined idea has no size and no plan, so any date attached to it would be a guess presented as a promise. Items in a 'Later' column signal direction, not delivery.

questions.explanation: A roadmap mixes items at very different levels of certainty, and stakeholders tend to read every item on it as a promise. A dated external commitment is defensible only where the work is understood, sized to fit the time available at observed velocity, and free of dependencies the team does not control. Checking each condition before agreeing a date keeps the roadmap a forecast and stops a partner agreement from turning a forecast into a contract.
questions.mindset: Commit dates only to work that is understood, sized and in the team's own hands.
